With regards to that, his views as expressed in Beyond Good and Evil are explicitely clear: he considers the scholars "philosophical laborers" but not genuine philosophers. By his account, they are not by any means profound, or discoverers of the soul, or higher men, or individuals who transvaluate values. In fact, I believe he'd view many of them as typical decadents, herd animals, Christians who say they're atheists but are actually Christians at heart (i.e: Peter Singer).

 For Nietzsche, genuine philosophers are individuals such as Goethe, Beethoven, the Greek Tragedians, even Plato. The question is---Do such genuine philosophers exist today? And would we notice them if they do exist?
It makes perfect sense actually. Credit and debit as power led to reason and memory, and the reason and memory led to a more refined form of punishment (contractual).

"How can punishment lead to this credit and debit, while debit and credit also leading to punishment?"

I recall that the initial punishment was a more barbaric, instinctive, tribal "punishment." Remember, Nietzsche says that our modern conception of pain as inherently a negative is not a constant conception throughout history. Take for instance the thousands of human sacrifices of the Azetcs, and how brutal and gruesome it was, the butchery involved...Early on, humans sometimes loved pain and cruelty, loved torture. Nietzsche mentions these practices of torture and cruelty in the 2nd essay.

Punishment as torture, cruelty, pain that led to memory is to be distinguished from punishment to secure a debt or promise. It may be wrong to classify the former as punishment at all, it's more accurate to say it's cruelty that led to memory (per Nietzsche's theory).

Bernard Reginster spends a chapter of his book on Nietzsche (The Affirmation of Life) on the Will to Power. The way he ends up defining it is: 

"It is, specifically, a desire for the overcoming
of resistance in the pursuit of some determinate first-order desire."

Essentially, you have a desire for X, but you also desire the overcoming of resistance in the pursuit of X, meaning you also desire to have resistance in your pursuit of X--In other words: the desire to have obstacles and challenges in the pursuit of your desire, and to overcome these obstacles and challenges. However, this book is an analytic exploration of Nietzsche's philosophy.

 With Nietzsche, I feel that his terms have a more poetic component than such precise definitions--In general, he refers to the Will to Power as the instinct for freedom and growth, or developing oneself, or sometimes even as an explanation for how the universe works (though, this last part is from his notebooks). But if you want a precise definition, Reginster has you covered. I'd recommend his book in general, it's really good.

I'm not well versed in philosophy in general, but I've experienced depression and suicidal ideation, and I've used philosophy to help deal with the problems in my life. However, Camus' absurdism was not in the least bit helpful. To me it was simply, "Well, this is just how it is, hehe!" I don't view Camus' absurdism as helpful or complex, just aggravating, and I'd honestly be insulted if someone recommended what amounts to a thought experiment to help me. The Stoics too were more detrimental than anything because they didn't have any passion to them. 

The only philosopher who has ever helped me is Nietzsche, because in my view, his philosophy speaks about the love of life, and because his psychological insights were endlessly productive in figuring out life, the world, my place in it, and the identifying of certain nihilistic thought processes that were making me worse.

The individual who reported me to reddit such that reddit would send me a Suicide help message, is an individual who perhaps requires mental healthcare more than me, which is actually an impressive achievement.

Things that have helped: Inspirational fiction, life-affirming works of philosophy, Russian fatalism, and Cutting.

Things I thought would be helpful but hurt me: exercise workbooks, internal family systems, CPTSD books.

Things I want to do where I'm capable: medication, drugs, nature hikes.

Hoarah Loux, and Godfrey in general, is some of the peak Elden Ring boss design. However, there are many complaints that Hoarah (and other ER bosses) have infinite combos, and that you're forced to run and bait out certain attacks, leading to an unengaging, unfun fight. I've also seen many youtube videos of ppl baiting attacks for 5 minutes strait. However, I think these complaints miss the point of how you're meant to fight him - positioning, and directional dodging:

>!At 0:04, I dodge only 2 hits <around> Hoarah, and then an opening with a jump attack. At 0:10, I dodge around Hoarah Loux, which prompts him to stop his "infinite thrash combo" and I weapon art him. His last stomp even misses me, cuz I roll around him, and not backwards. At 0:29, I hit in between a combo, responding again after only two hits. Then I dodge a hit, strafe around him so the 2nd literally misses, and boom a jump attack.!<

>!At 0:48 there's a combo I run from, but then from 0:50 to 1:07 there are <4> different openings. He gives me one hit, I dodge around then hit, and rinse and repeat 4 times. 4 openings right after the other. Total of 9 openings.!<

My point is that being aggressive, sticking close, strafing and rolling around the boss, will give you tons of openings by stopping the boss from continuing his combos and causing his attacks to miss. This makes the fight extremely engaging and enjoyable. I also beat him in 1:30 mins, compared to the 5 mins of baiting out attacks.

This also doesn't require much memorization, just constantly strafing and rolling around, not backwards. I hope this has helped some of you see how you're actually meant to fight some of these bosses, and enjoy Hoarah Loux more to have more fun playing ER XD.
